title: Element 11: Electricity
learningObjectives: Describe the factors that affect the severity of electric shock
Explain the main hazards from electrical systems in industrial workplaces
Outline safe practices for working on or near electrical equipment
Describe protection devices and their function

content.text: Electricity kills and injures in ways that are invisible and immediate. Even low voltages can be fatal depending on the circumstances. The factors that determine severity of injury are:

rows: Current (amps)
Most critical factor — 10 mA causes pain; 100 mA can be fatal; 1000 mA (1A) certain death
Voltage
Higher voltage → higher current through body. 50V AC or 120V DC are typically thresholds
Path through body
Through the heart or brain is most dangerous
Duration of contact
Longer contact = more energy delivered = greater harm
Body resistance
Wet skin has far lower resistance than dry skin — more current flows
Type of current
AC (alternating current) more dangerous than DC at equivalent voltages — causes tetanic muscle contraction

items: Electric shock — Current passing through the body; can cause cardiac arrest, respiratory failure, muscle damage
Burns — Electrical burns at contact points; arc flash burns (radiant heat)
Arc flash / arc blast — Electrical explosion at fault point; extreme temperatures (up to 20,000°C); UV/IR radiation; blast wave; molten metal droplets
Fire — Overheating cables, short circuits, sparks igniting flammables
Secondary hazards — Falls from height caused by shock-induced muscle contraction

content.text: A sudden, explosive release of energy caused by an electrical fault. Temperatures can reach 20,000°C — hotter than the surface of the sun. Arc flash can cause severe burns, blindness, hearing damage, and death. Workers working on live equipment must wear arc-rated (cal/cm²) PPE.

rows: Fuse
Melts and breaks circuit when current exceeds rated value
Overcurrent, short circuit — protects cables and equipment
Circuit Breaker (MCB/MCCB)
Trips automatically on overcurrent; can be reset
Overcurrent, short circuit
Residual Current Device (RCD)
Detects imbalance in current flow (indicates current going to earth/person); trips within 30 ms
Earth faults, electric shock — does NOT protect against direct contact between live conductors
Earth bonding
Connects metalwork to earth; fault current flows to earth not through person
Indirect contact shocks
Isolation transformer
Provides electrical separation; fault current has no return path through earth
Electric shock in high-risk wet areas

content.text: RCDs save lives. A 30mA RCD trips in less than 30ms — fast enough to prevent a fatal shock. All portable electrical equipment and work in wet/outdoor environments should be protected by RCDs. Test RCDs monthly using the test button.
The cardinal rule: always work dead (de-energised) where possible. Working live is only justified where it is unreasonable to de-energise, or where de-energisation itself introduces greater risk.

items: Dead working — Isolate, lock out (LOTO), prove dead with approved voltage tester before touching
Voltage tester — Use a two-pole voltage tester; test the tester works before and after proving dead
Isolation — Suitable means of isolation (not just switch); locked; danger tagged; posted
Competency — Only trained, authorised, competent persons work on electrical systems
Working live — Special permission required; insulated tools; rubber matting; arc flash PPE; no distractions
Temporary electrical installations — Must be inspected and tested; proper earthing; no overloading

content.text: 11.5 Overhead Power Lines and Underground Cables

items: Overhead lines — Main risk is equipment (cranes, excavators, tipper trucks) contacting lines. Controls: exclusion zones ('goal posts'), voltage confirmation, banksmen, permit to dig
Underground cables — Risk during excavation. Controls: plans from utility companies, CAT scanner/Genny, hand-dig near services, no mechanical breaking within 500mm of cable
Portable equipment — Regular visual checks; PAT testing; avoid coiling cables tightly (heat build-up)

content.text: High-voltage switchgear, substations, and electrical hazards are critical in Gulf petrochemical plants and power infrastructure. Aramco GI-0002.100 (Electrical Safety) mandates that all electrical work above 50V requires authorisation and an electrical isolation certificate. Arc flash studies must be conducted for all systems where live work may occur, and appropriate arc-flash PPE must be provided based on incident energy analysis.
